title: BioTIME v2 marine assemblages did not show larger richness gains with warming in warmer seas, in v1-era studies or in studies added in 2024 (23.5-60 degrees latitude)
abstract: Antao et al. (2020) used BioTIME v1 and reported that temperate marine species richness increased with local warming. They reported that this increase was about twice as large in warmer locations, that abundance decreased with warming in the warmest locations, and that land assemblages had no systematic response. We tested these claims in BioTIME 2.0. The 382 studies added in 2024 are an independent replication sample, and the 326 v1-era studies are a re-test. We built 22,996 assemblage time series (study x ~11 km cell, at least 5 years, 23.5-60 degrees latitude) from 374 studies. We rarefied each year to the minimum sample count of the series and calculated OLS slopes of log richness and log abundance. We regressed these slopes on the local temperature trend (NOAA ERSSTv5 for sea, GHCN_CAMS for land) and its interaction with baseline temperature, in 14 specifications. Marine richness had no overall link to warming: the pooled slope was +0.02 +- 0.10 log units per decade per 1 C/decade. The warming x baseline interaction was negative in 38 of 42 marine specifications and positive with p < 0.05 in none. This sign is opposite to the published claim. With inverse-variance weights, the v1-era interaction was -0.041 +- 0.007 per C, and it stayed in the range -0.043 to -0.032 when any one study was removed. In the 2024 studies, the interaction was -0.034 +- 0.023, which is not clear. The published abundance pattern occurred only with inverse-variance weights in v1-era data, depended on one trawl survey, had the opposite sign with equal study weights, and did not repeat in the 2024 studies. In each sample, the three largest surveys held 57-88% of the inverse-variance weight. Limitations: this is a re-implementation with different cells, temperature products and weights; the 2024 marine sample is small and mostly seabirds; and between-study confounding remains. The bundle has code, aggregate results and figures. Record-level BioTIME data remain outside the bundle.

Blue: equal weight per study; orange: inverse-variance random-effects weights. Bands are 95% study-clustered CIs; grey areas are outside the 5-95% range of the data. Antao et al. (2020) reported richness gains that increase with baseline temperature (a rising line); all richness lines are flat or falling.

Warming slope (left; at 15 C sea / 10 C land baseline) and warming x baseline interaction (right) for richness and abundance trends, by realm and sample, with 95% study-clustered CIs. Blue circles: equal weight per study; orange squares: inverse-variance weights.

Left: share of the total model weight held by the three largest studies under equal-study and inverse-variance weights. Right: marine warming x baseline interaction with all studies (marker) and its range when any one study is removed (bar).

citations.reason: Antao et al. 2020 reported temperature-related marine richness gains that were larger in warmer locations; we re-test this with BioTIME 2.0 and an independent 2024 study sample.
BioTIME 2.0 query RDS and metadata (15 April 2025) are the biodiversity data.
NOAA ERSSTv5 monthly SST for marine temperature trends.
NOAA GHCN_CAMS monthly land air temperature for land and freshwater trends.
HadISST 1.1 SST for a sensitivity analysis.
Blowes et al. 2019 used the same study x cell assemblage and rarefaction approach for BioTIME.
Dornelas et al. 2014 showed assemblage turnover without systematic richness loss in BioTIME precursor data.
